Extrapolate

/ik-STRAP-uh-layt/ - the stress falls on STRAP · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Extrapolate means to extend known information to estimate what is unknown.

Census planners extrapolate a county's population from the handful of blocks they can actually visit.

Worked Example

From the first hour of early voting — forty ballots, a steady line — the county clerk extrapolated the whole day's turnout, called two retired poll workers before lunch, and had extra chairs and a second scanner in place for the afternoon rush.

Extrapolate fits because the clerk stretched a measured trend past its last data point: one hour, extended to twelve. Infer would cover any conclusion drawn from evidence; predict says nothing about method. Extrapolate names the specific move — and its specific risk, since a trend may bend after the sample ends.

How Extrapolate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

project

project: runs current numbers forward — the business-page cousin

forecast

forecast: predicts what is coming, weather-report register

Antonyms

measure

measure: to read the value directly instead of estimating it

tally

tally: to count exactly what is in front of you, nothing beyond

How Strong Is It? — infer → extrapolate → conjecture

infer vs. extrapolate

infer vs. extrapolate: To infer is milder than to extrapolate: an inference rests directly on the evidence in front of you, while extrapolation stretches that evidence out past its edge.

conjecture vs. extrapolate

conjecture vs. extrapolate: Conjecture goes further than extrapolate — it leaps with hardly any data at all, where extrapolation at least follows a measured trend.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — extra-

Prefix — extra-: outside, beyond

Root — polate

Root — polate: to polish, to refurbish (Latin polire, borrowed whole from interpolate)

Put it together

Put it together: Extra- (beyond) + -polate (from Latin polire, “to polish up”) = to polish the data out beyond its edge. The word was built in the 1800s as a deliberate twin of interpolate — patching within the data — so extrapolate has meant “estimate beyond the data” from its first day on the job.

Use the root in a new word: interpolate

Use the root in a new word: interpolate: Rather than leave the graph blank, she interpolated Tuesday's missing temperature from Monday's and Wednesday's.

Root Check

Word Choice

technical

Extrapolate belongs to graphs, budgets, and forecasts — extending a known trend past its last data point. Where the unknown lies between known points, the word is interpolate; where there is no trend at all, you are only guessing.
